title: Dependency Injection — Service Lifetimes
blurb: Before the request can enter the controller, the container assembles it from registered services. Give each service the right lifetime — Singleton, Scoped, or Transient — or the assembly is subtly (sometimes invisibly) broken.

docs.label: Microsoft Learn — Dependency injection & service lifetimes

glossary.Singleton: One instance for the whole app, shared by every request and thread. Use for stateless, thread-safe, or expensive-to-build services.
glossary.Scoped: One instance per HTTP request, shared within that request. Use for per-request work like a DbContext — a unit of work that isn't thread-safe.
glossary.Transient: A brand-new instance every time it's requested. Use for lightweight, stateless helpers with no shared state.

levels.title: L1 · Pick the lifetime
levels.prompt: Read what each service is, then give it the right lifetime. The legend above explains each one.

items.label: AppDbContext
items.note: your EF Core unit of work; tracks changes for one request; not thread-safe

items.label: AppConfigCache
items.note: read-mostly settings shared by the whole app for its lifetime

items.label: EntityMapper
items.note: a tiny stateless helper with no fields; cheap to build

failStates.title: A Singleton DbContext leaks data
failStates.explain: As a Singleton the DbContext is shared across every request and thread. It isn't thread-safe, and its change-tracker never resets — so request #2 sees request #1's data. It must be Scoped: one unit of work per request.

failStates.title: Transient breaks the unit of work
failStates.explain: Transient hands out a fresh DbContext on every injection, so different components in the same request no longer share one transaction / change-tracker. A request should have a single unit of work — that's Scoped.

failStates.title: Don't rebuild shared state
failStates.explain: Rebuilding an app-wide cache on every resolve throws away the thing that makes it a cache. Shared, read-mostly state that lives for the app should be a Singleton.

failStates.title: A stateless helper doesn't need to be shared
failStates.explain: It would work, but a stateless helper has no shared state to protect, so it doesn't need one global instance. The convention is Transient — cheap, new each time.

levels.title: L2 · The trickier ones
levels.prompt: Same call, harder services — including per-request state and an expensive shared client.

items.label: CurrentUserContext
items.note: holds the signed-in user/tenant for THIS request

items.label: PaymentsApiClient
items.note: expensive to construct, thread-safe, reused across requests

items.label: OrderValidator
items.note: no state; checks one order and is done

items.label: AppDbContext
items.note: EF Core unit of work; not thread-safe

failStates.title: Per-request state can't be a Singleton
failStates.explain: A Singleton CurrentUserContext is shared across all requests, so user A's request could read user B's identity. Anything tied to the current request must be Scoped.

failStates.title: Transient loses the shared request view
failStates.explain: Transient gives each component its own CurrentUserContext, so they may disagree within one request. It should be one-per-request: Scoped.

failStates.title: Don't rebuild an expensive client
failStates.explain: Constructing a costly, thread-safe client on every request wastes work (and can exhaust sockets). Build it once and share it: Singleton.

failStates.title: Scoped still rebuilds too often
failStates.explain: Scoped makes a new client every request. Since it's thread-safe and expensive, one shared instance for the app is better: Singleton.

failStates.title: Stateless → Transient
failStates.explain: A stateless validator has nothing to share or protect, so a single global instance buys nothing. Transient is the convention.

levels.title: L3 · The captive dependency
levels.prompt: This app leaks data between requests. Find the bad registration and pick the fix.

payload.intro: Lifetimes must flow long → short down the graph: a long-lived service may only depend on equally- or longer-lived services.

fixes.label: Inject IServiceScopeFactory into CacheService; create a scope and resolve AppDbContext inside it per use
Register AppDbContext as a Singleton too

failStates.title: The DbContext's lifetime is correct
failStates.explain: AppDbContext SHOULD be Scoped — one unit of work per request. The bug is the Singleton that captures it, holding one DbContext alive forever and leaking data across requests.

failStates.title: The Transient mapper is fine
failStates.explain: A Transient has the shortest life, so nothing captures it here. Look for a long-lived service depending on a shorter-lived one.

failStates.title: That makes the leak permanent
failStates.explain: Promoting AppDbContext to Singleton means one shared, non-thread-safe DbContext for the whole app — the captive-dependency disaster made official. Never lengthen the captive's life.

failStates.title: That throws away the cache
failStates.explain: A Transient cache is rebuilt on every resolve, so it caches nothing. Keep CacheService a Singleton and pull a fresh DbContext from a created scope only when it needs one.
